title: Recent Calls

concept.title: A queue of times: old ones leave from the front
body: A counter answers "how many calls came in the last 3000 milliseconds?". Calls arrive with increasing times. Keep the times of the **recent** calls in a queue. A new call joins at the back. Calls that are too old are removed from the **front**; because times only grow, the oldest call is always at the front and nothing older can hide behind a newer one.

body.code:
window = deque()
for t in times:
    window.append(t)
    while window[0] < t - 3000:      # the front is the oldest call
        window.popleft()
    print(len(window))

body: Every call enters once and leaves once, so the work is O(n) in total. In Python use `collections.deque` (a plain list is slow at removing from the front); C++ has `queue` and `deque`, Java has `ArrayDeque`.

statement: A counter records calls at the given times (in milliseconds), in strictly increasing order. After each call, print how many calls (including this one) happened in the time range `[t - 3000, t]`, where `t` is the time of this call.
inputFormat: The second line has the `n` times, strictly increasing.

examples.note: At 3001 the range is [1, 3001]: 3 calls. At 3002 the range is [2, 3002]: the call at 1 is too old: 3 calls.

hints: Keep the times of the recent calls in a queue.
Remove from the front while the oldest time is smaller than `t - 3000`.
The answer is the size of the queue.

explanation: The queue holds the times of the calls in the window. Too old calls are removed from the front; the size of the queue is the answer.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
t = list(map(int, input().split()))

from collections import deque
window = deque()
out = []
for x in t:
    window.append(x)
    while window[0] < x - 3000:
        window.popleft()
    out.append(len(window))
print(*out)
